# Statistics in the media - Practice Test - Year 10

Attempt all questions and show your working. Suggested time: 30 to 35 minutes.

## Section A: Consolidating (Questions 1-4)

**Question 1**

A news report says, "Sales of electric bikes rose from 2000 last year to 2500 this year."

By what percentage did sales increase?

**Question 2**

A TV advertisement says, "80% of customers prefer our coffee!" The fine print says 10 customers were asked.

(a) How many of the customers asked preferred the coffee?

(b) Give one reason why this claim is not convincing.

**Question 3**

The five houses sold in a street last year sold for:

\$600 000, \$620 000, \$650 000, \$680 000, \$2 900 000

(a) Find the mean sale price.

(b) Find the median sale price.

(c) A newspaper reports the mean as the "typical" price in the street. Which measure better describes a typical price? Explain.

**Question 4**

A headline reads: "Students who eat breakfast get better marks, so breakfast makes you smarter."

Explain why the conclusion in this headline may not be valid.

## Section B: Standard (Questions 5-16)

**Question 5**

A company's annual report shows a column graph of its profit. The vertical axis starts at \$9 million and goes up to \$10 million. The profit was \$9.2 million in 2024 and \$9.6 million in 2025.

(a) Find the actual percentage increase in profit, correct to one decimal place.

(b) How many times taller does the 2025 column look than the 2024 column?

(c) Explain why the graph is misleading.

**Question 6**

The unemployment rate in a region rose from 4% to 5%.

Report A says, "Unemployment rose by 1%." Report B says, "Unemployment rose by 25%."

Explain what each report means, and suggest clearer wording for Report A.

**Question 7**

A headline says, "Common habit DOUBLES your risk of rare illness!" The study found the risk rose from 2 in 10 000 people to 4 in 10 000 people.

(a) By how many people in 10 000 did the risk increase?

(b) Write the original risk and the new risk as percentages.

(c) Explain why the headline may cause more worry than the numbers justify.

**Question 8**

A company's share price at the start of each month was:

| Month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | \$5.00 | \$4.60 | \$4.10 | \$3.80 | \$4.00 | \$4.30 |

An advertisement for the shares says, "Our share price rose 13% in just two months!"

(a) Which two months is the advertisement comparing? Check that the 13% figure is correct (to the nearest whole number).

(b) Find the percentage change in price from January to June.

(c) Explain why the advertisement is misleading.

**Question 9**

A local council wants to know how residents feel about public transport. It puts a survey on its website and posts the link on its social media page.

(a) Identify two groups of residents who may be under-represented in the results.

(b) Explain how this could make the results biased.

**Question 10**

A fitness app collects the location of its users so it can publish statistics about how busy different gyms are.

Describe two ethical issues the company should consider when collecting and publishing this data.

**Question 11**

A study reports that drinking soft drink has no effect on weight gain. The study was paid for by a soft drink company.

(a) Why should readers be careful about this conclusion?

(b) What information about the study would help you decide whether to trust it?

**Question 12**

A report states: "Based on a random sample of 1200 adults, 63% support a four-day working week."

(a) How many adults in the sample supported a four-day week?

(b) List two pieces of information that are missing from the report and would help you judge the claim.

(c) Is it reasonable to conclude that a majority of all adults support a four-day week? Explain.

**Question 13**

A small business has 10 employees. Eight earn \$55 000 a year, the manager earns \$150 000 and the owner earns \$360 000. A job advertisement says, "Our average salary is \$95 000!"

(a) Show that the mean salary is \$95 000.

(b) Find the median salary.

(c) Which value gives a fairer picture of what a new employee is likely to earn? Explain.

**Question 14**

A survey of 50 students at one city school found they spend an average of 5 hours a day on their phones. A news article reports, "Australian teenagers spend 5 hours a day on their phones."

Give two reasons why this conclusion may not be valid.

**Question 15**

A newspaper shows spending on a project with two pictures of money bags. Spending doubled, so the second bag is drawn twice as tall and twice as wide as the first bag.

(a) How many times larger does the area of the second bag look?

(b) Explain why this picture is misleading.

**Question 16**

A headline reads, "Burglaries in our suburb up 50%!" Last year there were 4 burglaries in the suburb. This year there were 6.

(a) Check the 50% figure.

(b) Explain why the headline may give a misleading impression.

## Section C: Advanced (Questions 17-20)

**Question 17**

A magazine posted survey forms to all 20 000 of its subscribers. 1600 forms were returned, and 75% of the returned forms said the reader was happy with the magazine.

The magazine then printed the headline: "75% of our readers are happy!"

(a) What percentage of the survey forms were returned?

(b) How many of the returned forms said the reader was happy?

(c) What percentage of all 20 000 subscribers are known to be happy?

(d) Explain why the headline may be biased.

**Question 18**

Last year City A had 120 car thefts and City B had 80 car thefts. A headline says, "City A is the car theft capital!"

City A has a population of 400 000 and City B has a population of 200 000.

(a) Find the number of car thefts per 10 000 people in each city.

(b) Is the headline justified? Explain.

**Question 19**

A sports drink company set up a stall at a marathon. It asked 40 people who visited the stall whether its drink improved their performance; 36 said yes. Its advertisement now says, "90% of athletes say our drink improves performance!"

(a) Check the 90% figure.

(b) Describe three problems with how this conclusion was reached.

(c) Describe a fairer way to test whether the drink improves performance.

**Question 20**

A report says: "Since new speed cameras were installed on a highway, crashes fell from 50 last year to 35 this year. The cameras have cut crashes by 30%."

(a) Check the 30% figure.

(b) Give two other possible reasons why the number of crashes might have fallen.

(c) What extra data would make the claim more convincing?

# Statistics in the media - Answer Key

**Question 1**

Answer: $25\%$ ($\frac{500}{2000} \times 100$)

**Question 2**

Answer: (a) $8$ (b) The sample is very small (only 10 people), so the result could easily be due to chance. (Also accept: we don't know how the customers were chosen, or the company ran the survey itself.)

**Question 3**

Answer: (a) \$1 090 000 (b) \$650 000 (c) The median, because the one very expensive house (\$2 900 000) pulls the mean up above four of the five prices.

**Question 4**

Answer: An association does not prove causation. Other factors, such as more sleep, family routines or support at home, could explain both eating breakfast and getting better marks.

**Question 5**

Answer: (a) $4.3\%$ ($\frac{0.4}{9.2} \times 100$) (b) $3$ times (heights above \$9 million are $0.6$ and $0.2$) (c) Because the axis does not start at zero, a small increase of about $4\%$ looks like the profit tripled.

**Question 6**

Answer: The rate went up by 1 percentage point (Report A), which is a $25\%$ increase relative to the original 4% (Report B). Clearer wording for A: 'rose by 1 percentage point' (or 'rose from 4% to 5%').

**Question 7**

Answer: (a) $2$ in $10\,000$ (b) $0.02\%$ and $0.04\%$ (c) 'Doubles' is a relative increase; the actual risk is still very small (4 in 10 000), and only 2 extra people in 10 000 are affected.

**Question 8**

Answer: (a) April to June: $\frac{0.50}{3.80} \times 100 \approx 13\%$ (b) a decrease of $14\%$ (c) It picks only the time period that looks good; over the whole six months the price fell by $14\%$.

**Question 9**

Answer: (a) Any two, such as: people who don't visit the council website or social media, older residents, people without internet access, people who are busy or not interested. (b) The people who respond may not be typical of all residents (for example, people with strong opinions are more likely to respond), so the results may not reflect the whole population.

**Question 10**

Answer: Any two, such as: users must give informed consent to their location being collected; data must be anonymous so individuals can't be identified or tracked; data must be stored securely; data should only be used for the purpose users agreed to.

**Question 11**

Answer: (a) The company has a conflict of interest and benefits from this result, so the study may be biased in its design or reporting. (b) Any two, such as: the sample size, how participants were chosen, how long the study lasted, whether it was published or checked by independent experts, whether other independent studies agree.

**Question 12**

Answer: (a) $756$ (b) Any two, such as: the exact question asked, who ran or paid for the survey, how the sample was chosen and where, how many people refused to answer. (c) Yes, it is reasonable: the sample is large and random and 63% is well above 50%, although the result is still an estimate.

**Question 13**

Answer: (a) $\frac{8 \times 55\,000 + 150\,000 + 360\,000}{10} = \frac{950\,000}{10} = 95\,000$ (b) \$55 000 (c) The median, because most employees earn \$55 000 and the two high salaries pull the mean up.

**Question 14**

Answer: Any two, such as: the sample is small (50 students); all students came from one school, so they may not represent teenagers in other places (for example country areas); the students may not have been chosen randomly; self-reported phone time may be inaccurate.

**Question 15**

Answer: (a) $4$ times ($2 \times 2$) (b) The amount only doubled, but the picture's area is 4 times as large, which makes the increase look much bigger than it is.

**Question 16**

Answer: (a) $\frac{6 - 4}{4} \times 100 = 50\%$, correct (b) The actual numbers are very small (an increase of only 2), so a big percentage change can happen by chance; the headline makes it sound like a large crime wave.

**Question 17**

Answer: (a) $8\%$ (b) $1200$ (c) $6\%$ (d) Only $8\%$ replied, and people who chose to reply may feel differently from those who didn't (non-response or voluntary response bias), so $75\%$ may not represent all readers.

**Question 18**

Answer: (a) City A: $3$ per $10\,000$; City B: $4$ per $10\,000$ (b) No. City A has more thefts only because it has more people; the rate of car theft is higher in City B.

**Question 19**

Answer: (a) $\frac{36}{40} \times 100 = 90\%$ (b) Any three, such as: small sample; people who visited the stall were self-selected and may already like the drink; the company ran the survey and benefits from the result; people may give the answer they think is wanted; opinions are not measurements of performance. (c) For example: randomly split a large group of athletes, give one group the drink and the other a similar-tasting drink without the ingredient (without telling them which), and compare measured times.

**Question 20**

Answer: (a) $\frac{50 - 35}{50} \times 100 = 30\%$, correct (b) Any two, such as: less traffic, better weather, road repairs, a new lower speed limit, safer cars, natural year-to-year variation. (c) Crash data for several years before and after, and data from similar roads without cameras over the same period (and traffic volumes).
check_notes: All percentages, means, medians, rates and ratios recomputed in Python; open-response answers re-read against each question and written as key points with accepted alternatives.
